title: The Science of Sleep Cycles: Why You Wake Up Tired

slides.heading: Why Do You Wake Up Tired?
slides.body: The hidden science of sleep cycles — and how to finally wake up refreshed

slides.heading: Sleep Isn't One Long State
slides.body: Your brain cycles through distinct stages throughout the night. Each full cycle lasts about 90 minutes and repeats 4–6 times. Missing or cutting short these cycles is the main reason you feel groggy in the morning.

slides.heading: The 4 Stages of Sleep
slides.body: Stage 1 is light drowsiness. Stage 2 is true light sleep where your heart rate slows. Stages 3–4 are deep slow-wave sleep — the most physically restorative. REM sleep follows, when dreaming and memory consolidation happen.

slides.heading: What Happens in Deep Sleep
slides.body: During deep sleep, your body releases growth hormone to repair tissues and muscles. Blood pressure drops and immune function strengthens. This stage is hardest to wake from — being jolted out of it causes intense sleep inertia (that foggy, confused feeling).

slides.heading: REM: The Brain's Overnight Workshop
slides.body: Rapid Eye Movement sleep is when your brain processes emotions and consolidates memories. Your body is temporarily paralyzed to stop you acting out dreams. Adults spend about 20–25% of total sleep in REM, with longer REM periods toward morning.

slides.heading: Why Timing Your Alarm Matters
slides.body: Waking mid-cycle — especially during deep sleep — triggers sleep inertia that can last 30–60 minutes. Waking at the end of a 90-minute cycle, when sleep is lightest, feels far easier. That's why 7.5 hours (5 cycles) often beats 8 hours of poorly timed sleep.

slides.heading: Sleep Debt: It Compounds Fast
slides.body: Losing even 60–90 minutes of sleep a night has measurable effects on attention, mood, and decision-making within days. Unlike financial debt, you can't fully 'pay back' severe sleep debt — chronic loss causes lasting cognitive impairment.

slides.heading: Alcohol and Sleep Quality
slides.body: Alcohol helps you fall asleep faster but fragments the second half of your night. It suppresses REM sleep and causes more awakenings. Even moderate drinking before bed can reduce sleep quality by up to 40%, explaining that exhausted-after-drinking feeling.

slides.heading: Simple Hacks to Wake Up Better
slides.body: Keep a consistent wake time — even on weekends — to anchor your circadian rhythm. Get bright light within 30 minutes of waking to suppress residual melatonin. Avoid screens 60 minutes before bed and keep your bedroom cool (around 18°C / 65°F).

slides.heading: Sleep Smarter, Not Longer
slides.body: Quality beats quantity. Protect your sleep cycles, time your alarms wisely, and your body will do the rest. Great sleep is the highest-ROI habit you can build — your brain and body will thank you.
